source_text:
uos enim nostis, temere credentibus quam uehementer insultare soleatis, praesertim cum ipse, qui iam coepit incerta narrare, plenam ac firmam scientiam paulo ante promiserit
Deinde quoniam, si mihi fides imperanda est, magis me terret illa scriptura, ubi lego uenisse spiritum sanctum et apostolos inspirasse, quibus eum dominus se missurum esse promiserat. quapropter aut ea, quae dicit, proba mihi uera esse, ut ostendas, quae non possum credere, aut eum, qui dicit, proba mihi spiritum sanctum esse, ut credam, quae non potes ostendere. ego namque catholicam fidem profiteor et per illam me ad certam scientiam peruenturum esse praesumo; tu uero, qui fidem meam labefactare conaris, certam scientiam trade, si potes, ut id, quod credidi, temere me credidisse conuincas. duo sunt, quae mihi profers: unum, cum dicis spiritum sanctum esse, qui loquitur, et alterum, cum dicis manifesta esse, quae loquitur. utrumque abs te sine ulla dubitatione cognoscere debui; sed non sum auarus, unum horum doce. ostende hunc esse spiritum sanctum, et credam uera esse, quae dicit, etiamsi nesciam; aut ostende uera esse, quae dicit, et credam spiritum sanctum esse, etiamsi nesciam. numquid aequius aut beniuolentius tecum agi potest? sed tu nec hoc nec illud uales ostendere. nihil aliud elegisti nisi laudare, quod credis, et inridere, quod credo. cum igitur etiam ego uicissim laudauero, quod credo et quod credis, inrisero, quid putas nobis esse iudicandum quidue faciendum, nisi ut eos relinquamus, qui nos inuitant certa cognoscere et postea imperant, ut incerta credamus et eos sequamur, qui nos inuitant prius credere, quod nondum ualemus intueri, ut ipsa fide ualentiores facti, quod credimus, intellegere mereamur, non iam hominibus, sed ipso deo intrinsecus mentem nostram inluminante atque firmante ?
Et quoniam quaesiui, unde mihi probet, nunc quaero, unde ipse cognouerit. si dicit sibi esse spiritu sancto reuelatum suamque mentem diuinitus inlustratam, ut ea, quae dicit, certa et manifesta cognosceret, ipse significat, quid intersit inter cognoscere et credere. ipse enim cognoscit, cui apertissime ista monstrantur; eis autem, quibus haec narrat, non cognitionem insinuat, sed credulitatem suadet. cui quisquis temere consenserit, Manichaeus efficitur, non certa cognoscendo, sed incerta credendo, quales nos inperitos adulescentulos aliquando decepit. debuit ergo non nobis polliceri scientiam neque manifestam cognitionem neque ad id. quod quaeritur, sine ulla ambiguitate peruentionem, sed dicere potius sibi esse ista monstrata, illos autem, quibus narrantur, credere sibi debere, quae nesciunt. sed si hoc diceret, quis non ei responderet: si ergo incognita crediturus sum, cur non ea potius credam, quae iam consensione doctorum indoctorumque celebrantur et per omnes populos grauissima auctoritate firmata sunt? hoc ille metuens ne sibi diceretur, offundit nebulas inperitis, primum pollicens rerum certarum cognitionem, postea et incertarum imperans fidem. cui tamen si hoc dicatur, ut saltem uel sibi haec doceat esse monstrata, similiter deficit et hoc quoque ut credamus iubet. quis ferat tantam fallaciam tantamque superbiam?
thought_title: Faith and knowledge: Mani cannot prove either his Spirit-claim or his message
orientation: Augustine is addressing Mani directly, challenging the claim that Mani is the Paraclete and that his teachings are certain knowledge rather than objects of faith.
pass_a_gloss: you [pl.] for know, to [those] rashly believing how vehemently to insult you [pl.] are accustomed, especially when he himself, who already began uncertain [things] to narrate, full and firm knowledge a little before promised. Then since, if to me faith is to be commanded, more me terrifies that scripture, where I read [that] came [the] Holy Spirit and [the] apostles inspired, to whom him [the] Lord himself [that] he would send had promised. Wherefore either those [things], which he says, prove to me true to be, that you may show, which I cannot believe, or him, who speaks, prove to me [the] Holy Spirit to be, that I may believe, which you cannot show. I indeed [the] catholic faith profess and through it me to certain knowledge to arrive I presume; you however, who my faith to weaken you try, certain knowledge hand over, if you can, that that, which I believed, rashly me to have believed you may convict. Two are, which to me you bring forward: one, when you say [the] Holy Spirit to be, who speaks, and [the] other, when you say manifest to be, which he speaks. Both from you without any doubt to know I ought; but not I am greedy, one of these teach. Show this [one] to be [the] Holy Spirit, and I will believe true to be, which he says, even if I may not know; or show true to be, which he says, and I will believe [the] Holy Spirit to be, even if I may not know. Surely more fairly or more kindly with you to be dealt can? But you neither this nor that are able to show. Nothing else you chose except to praise, what you believe, and to mock, what I believe. When therefore also I in turn will have praised, what I believe and what you believe, will have mocked, what do you think for us to be judged or what to be done, unless that those we leave, who us invite certain [things] to know and afterwards command, that uncertain [things] we believe, and those we follow, who us invite first to believe, what not yet we are able to see, that by that faith made stronger, what we believe, to understand we may deserve, not now by men, but by God himself inwardly our mind illuminating and strengthening? And since I asked, whence to me he proves, now I ask, whence he himself knew. If he says to himself to be by [the] Holy Spirit revealed and his mind divinely illuminated, that those [things], which he says, certain and manifest he might know, he himself signifies, what lies between between to know and to believe. He himself for knows, to whom most openly these [things] are shown; to those however, to whom these [things] he narrates, not knowledge he introduces, but belief he persuades. To whom whoever rashly will have agreed, a Manichaean is made, not certain [things] by knowing, but uncertain [things] by believing, such as us inexperienced young men once he deceived. He ought therefore not to us to promise knowledge nor manifest cognition nor to that, which is sought, without any ambiguity arrival, but to say rather to himself to be these [things] shown, those however, to whom they are narrated, to believe him to owe, which they do not know. But if this he said, who not to him would answer: if therefore unknown [things] I am going to believe, why not those rather I should believe, which already by agreement of learned and unlearned are celebrated and through all peoples by most weighty authority have been strengthened? This he fearing lest to him it be said, pours clouds over [the] inexperienced, first promising of certain things knowledge, afterwards also of uncertain [things] commanding faith. To whom nevertheless if this is said, that at least even to himself these [things] he may teach to have been shown, similarly he fails and this too that we believe he orders. Who would bear so great deceit and so great pride?

choices.why: Keeps the adverbial force of 'temere' (rashly) with the participle, matching Augustine's repeated contrast between rash belief and certain knowledge.
Preserves the two adjectives as coordinate, emphasizing Mani's earlier promise of complete certainty.

choices.english: faith is to be commanded to me
choices.why: The gerundive with dative of agent keeps the passive obligation and the sense that faith is being imposed on Augustine.
rejected: I must be commanded to have faith

choices.why: 'Trade' is an imperative with the sense of delivering or handing over; 'certain knowledge' preserves the key contrast with 'incerta' (uncertain things).

choices.english: he pours clouds over the inexperienced
choices.why: The metaphor of pouring clouds (obscuring) is kept literal, and 'inexperienced' renders 'inperitis' as those lacking skill or knowledge.
rejected: he casts fog over the ignorant
he spreads clouds over the unskilled

choices.term: non cognitionem insinuat, sed credulitatem suadet
choices.english: he does not instill knowledge, but persuades belief
choices.why: 'Insinuat' has the sense of introducing or instilling gradually; 'credulitatem' is rendered as 'belief' to keep the contrast with 'cognitionem' (knowledge).
rejected: he does not impart knowledge, but urges credulity
he does not teach knowledge, but persuades belief

bible_refs.note: uenisse spiritum sanctum et apostolos inspirasse
quibus eum dominus se missurum esse promiserat

pass_b_english: You yourselves know how fiercely you are in the habit of insulting those who believe rashly, especially since the very man who has now begun to narrate uncertain things promised a full and firm knowledge a little earlier.

Then again, if faith is to be commanded to me, I am more frightened by that Scripture where I read that the Holy Spirit came and inspired the apostles, to whom the Lord had promised he would send him (Acts 2:1-4; John 14:26). Therefore either prove to me that the things he says are true, so that you may show what I cannot believe, or prove to me that the one who speaks is the Holy Spirit, so that I may believe what you cannot show.

For my part, I profess the Catholic faith, and through it I presume that I will arrive at certain knowledge. But you, who try to weaken my faith, hand over certain knowledge if you can, so that you may convict me of having believed rashly what I believed. There are two things you offer me: one, when you say that the one who speaks is the Holy Spirit, and the other, when you say that the things he speaks are manifest. I ought to know both from you without any doubt; but I am not greedy—teach me one of them. Show that this man is the Holy Spirit, and I will believe that what he says is true, even if I do not know it; or show that what he says is true, and I will believe that he is the Holy Spirit, even if I do not know it. Could anyone deal with you more fairly or more kindly? But you can show neither the one nor the other. You have chosen nothing else but to praise what you believe and ridicule what I believe.

Since I in turn will have praised what I believe and ridiculed what you believe, what do you think we should judge or do, except to abandon those who invite us to know certain things and afterward command us to believe uncertain things, and to follow those who invite us first to believe what we are not yet able to see, so that, made stronger by that very faith, we may merit to understand what we believe—no longer through men, but through God himself illuminating and strengthening our mind within?

And since I have asked how he proves it to me, I now ask how he himself came to know it. If he says that it was revealed to him by the Holy Spirit and that his mind was divinely illuminated so that he might know the things he says as certain and manifest, he himself indicates what the difference is between knowing and believing. For he himself knows, since these things are shown to him most openly; but to those to whom he narrates them, he does not instill knowledge, but persuades belief. Whoever rashly agrees with him becomes a Manichaean, not by knowing certain things, but by believing uncertain things—just as he once deceived us when we were inexperienced young men.

Therefore he ought not to have promised us knowledge, nor manifest cognition, nor arrival at the matter in question without any ambiguity, but rather to say that these things were shown to him, and that those to whom they are narrated ought to believe him about things they do not know. But if he said that, who would not answer him: If I am going to believe unknown things, why should I not rather believe those things that are already celebrated by the agreement of learned and unlearned alike and are established among all peoples by the weightiest authority? Fearing that this would be said to him, he pours clouds over the inexperienced, first promising knowledge of certain things, and afterward commanding faith in uncertain things. Yet if this is said to him—that he should at least teach that these things were shown even to himself—he likewise fails, and orders us to believe this too. Who could bear such deceit and such arrogance?

dismissed.quote: Since I in turn will have praised what I believe and ridiculed what you believe
dismissed.why: The Latin 'et quod credis' is object of 'inrisero' (I will have ridiculed), not 'laudauero.' Augustine says he will praise what he believes AND ridicule what Mani believes.
dismissed.note: The English already pairs praise with 'what I believe' and ridicule with 'what you believe', and the proposed fix is identical to it.

last_rejected.source_quote: quibus eum dominus se missurum esse promiserat
last_rejected.why: John 14:26 has the Father send the Spirit. The Latin says the Lord promised he himself would send him (John 15:26 or 16:7).
last_rejected.fix: Cite John 15:26 or 16:7 for the Lord’s promise that he would send the Spirit.
last_rejected.ruling: Citation is a parenthetical gloss; John 14:26 says the Father will send the Spirit in Christ's name, and the 'quibus eum dominus se missurum' idea fits John 15:26/16:7 better, but this is minor.
